extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, psychophysicists, and experimental anthropologists conducting sensory discrimination and mental-imagery investigations
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and conducting psychophysical tests of tactile weight-discrimination and auditory upper-limit hearing (whistles), plus administering a questionnaire to elicit and grade visualising and allied mental faculties. Includes apparatus design, trial procedures, scoring/interpretation rules, and question-by-question dimensions for imagery assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of test-weights in geometric series (Weber's law)
rubrics_metrics.description: I use test-weights that mount in a series of 'just perceptible differences' ... their values being calculated according to Weber's law. The lowest weight is heavy enough to give a decided sense of weight ... and the heaviest weight can be handled without any sense of fatigue. They therefore conform with close approximation to a geometric series; thus-- WR0, WR1, WR2, WR3, etc., and they bear as register-marks the values of the successive indices, 0, 1, 2, 3, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the series is geometric, if a person can just distinguish between weights whose register-marks differ by a certain amount, he should be able to distinguish any other pair with the same register difference. This underpins comparability of tests across different parts of the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of relative sensitivity (comparative dulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be but one interpretation of the phrase that the dulness of muscular sense in any person, B, is twice as great as in that of another person, A. It is that B is only capable of perceiving one grade of difference where A can perceive two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express relative sensitivity inversely (sensitivity rather than dulness): e.g., if A can distinguish a difference of 2 marks and B only 4 marks, B's dulness is twice A's. This interpretation is independent of the particular pair of weights used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion between apparatus scales
rubrics_metrics.description: The conversion of results obtained by the use of one series of test-weights into what would have been given by another series, is a piece of simple arithmetic ... In my own apparatus the unit of weight is 2 per cent.; ... In another apparatus the unit of weight might be 3 per cent., then three grades of mine would be equal to two of the other, and mine would be converted to that scale by multiplying them by 2/3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the unit (percent difference) of the apparatus used. Convert results between apparatus by multiplying by the ratio of their units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient trials and tray size to reduce chance
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient number of test-weights must be used, or trials made, to eliminate the influence of chance. ... I prefer to use trays, each containing only three weights, the trials being made three or four times in succession. In each trial there are three possibilities and only one success, therefore in three trials the probabilities against uniform success are as 27 to 1, and in four trials at 81 to 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triplets (three weights per tray) and repeat trials 3–4 times to make accidental correct sequences unlikely. The arithmetic of permutations is used to justify this tray size and trial number rather than naive factorial estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable error patterns in ordering trials (permissible permutations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person is tested, an approximate value for his grade of sensitivity is rapidly found, and the inquiry becomes narrowed to finding out whether he can surely pass a particular mistake. ... If he had three weights to arrange in their consecutive order, 1, 2, 3, there are 3×2 = 6 ways of arranging them; of these, he would be liable to the errors of 1, 3, 2, and of 2, 1, 3, but he would hardly be liable to such gross errors as 2, 3, 1, or 3, 2, 1, or 3, 1, 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scoring, discount highly implausible permutations as not representative of chance; focus on likely near-miss errors when estimating a subject's sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting visual cues: restriction of varieties and use of bags
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason of this limitation of varieties was to enable the weights to be interchanged whenever there became reason to suspect that the eye had begun to recognise the appearance of any one of them, and that the judgment might be influenced by that recognition, and cease to be wholly guided by the sense of weight. ... The most perfect way would be to drop the weights, each in a little bag or sheath of light material, so that the operatee could not see the weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only a limited number of visual varieties among weights and interchange them; employ small bags or sheaths (kept in the box) when necessary to eliminate visual recognition and confirm tactile judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of weight values and register marking
rubrics_metrics.description: After preparatory trials, I adopted 1000 grains as the value of W and 1020 as that of R, but I am now inclined to think that 1010 would have been better. ... There are thirty weights in all, but only ten varieties, whose Register Numbers are respectively 0, 1, 2, 3, 3-1/2, 4-1/2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12. The cartridge whose weight was WR4 was marked 4'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a base unit and mark register-numbers on cartridges; include half-step units if desired. Keep a record of chosen register numbers and be prepared to adjust the base unit after pilot trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of weights into trays with grade markings
rubrics_metrics.description: The weights are placed in sets of threes, each set in a separate shallow tray, and the trays lie in two rows in a box. Each tray bears the register-marks of each of the weights it contains. It is also marked boldly with a Roman numeral showing the difference between the register-marks of the adjacent weights. This difference indicates the grade of sensitivity that the weights in the tray are designed to test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise trays so each triplet targets a particular grade of sensitivity; mark trays with register-marks and a grade numeral to standardise which sensitivity grade is being tested in each trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred sequences for triplet trays (grade-to-sequence mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table mapping 'Just perceptible Ratio' → 'Grade of Sensitivity' → 'Sequences of Weights' (e.g., 1.020 → I. → 1,2,3; 1.030 → I.1/2 → 2,3-1/2,5; 1.040 → II. → 3,5,7; ... 1.127 → VI. → 0,6,12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided sequences as templates when preparing trays for specific sensitivity grades. Half-step sequences and doublets can be used to obtain intermediate or coarser tests up to a maximum difference (e.g., XII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation and subject posture/handling procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A tray is taken out, the three weights that it contains is shuffled by the operator who then passes them on to the experimenter. The latter sits at ease with his hand in an unconstrained position, and lifts the weights in turn between his finger and thumb, the finger pressing against the top, the thumb against the bottom of the cartridge. Guided by the touch alone, he arranges them in the tray in what he conceives to be their proper sequence; he then returns the tray to the operator, who notes the result, the operator then reshuffles the weights and repeats the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the subject's hand posture and lifting method are standardised (finger top, thumb bottom). Operator should shuffle and reseal between trials; subject must be guided to rely on touch only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory tests, recording onset, and stopping criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to begin with coarse preparatory tests, to accustom the operatee to the character of the work. After a minute or two the operator may begin to record results, and the testing may go for several minutes, until the hand begins to tire, the judgment to be confused, and blunders to arise. Practice does not seem to increase the delicacy of perception after the first few trials, so much as might be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with coarse trials as practice. Begin formal recording after brief familiarisation (1–2 minutes). Stop testing when fatigue or confusion produces more errors; do not expect large gains from long practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of doublets and maximum coarse differences for diminished sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Again, that it is easy to select doublets of weights for coarser tests, up to a maximum difference of XII., which may be useful in cases of morbidly diminished sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects with severely reduced tactile sensitivity, use pairs (doublets) with larger register differences (up to XII) to obtain measurable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistle construction with adjustable inner tube by screw plug
rubrics_metrics.description: The base of the inner tube of the whistle is the foremost end of a plug, that admits of being advanced or withdrawn by screwing it out or in; thus the depth of the inner tube of the whistle can be varied at pleasure. The depth of the inner tube of the whistle at any moment is shown by the graduations on the outside of the instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design whistles with a screw-adjustable plug so depth (and therefore pitch) is continuously variable and graduations are readable from scale and cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale unit and reading convention for whistles (1/250 inch unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: For mechanical convenience, a screw is used whose pitch is 25 to the inch; ... The edge of the cap is divided into ten parts, each of which corresponds to the tenth of a complete turn; and, therefore, to one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of an inch. Hence in reading off the graduations the tens are shown on the body of the whistle, and the units are shown on the edge of the cap. The scale of the instrument having for its unit the two-hundred-and-fiftieth part of an inch ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate and read the scale using tenths on cap + tens on body to obtain 1/250 inch precision; record the scale reading used for each test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula to compute vibrations per second from scale reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of vibrations in the note of the whistle may be found by dividing 13,440 by four times the depth, measured in inches ... The scale unit being 1/250 of an inch, the number of vibrations in the note of the whistle is to be found by dividing (13440 x 250)/4 or 84,000, by the graduations read off on its scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute frequency (vibrations/sec) as 84,000 divided by the scale reading (in units of 1/250 inch). Use the table provided to map readings to vibration counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pipe theory and the effect of bore vs depth
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule ... ceases to apply when the depth of the tube is less than about one and a half times its diameter. When the tube is reduced to a shallow pan, a note may still be produced by it, but that note has reference rather to the diameter of the whistle than to its depth, being sometimes apparently unaltered by a further decrease of depth. The necessity of preserving a fair proportion between the diameter and the depth of a whistle is the reason why these instruments, having necessarily little depth, require to be made with very small bores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For high-frequency tests, maintain appropriate depth-to-diameter proportions; beware that when depth < ~1.5×diameter, formulaic frequency estimates are unreliable and diameter begins to govern the note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical bore/depth guidance and safe upper-frequency estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest whistles suitable for experiments on the human ear, have an inner tube of about 0.16 inches in diameter, which is equal to 40 units of the scale. Consequently in these instruments the theory of closed pipes ceases to be trustworthy when the depth of the whistle is less than about 60 units. In short, we cannot be sure of sounding with them a higher note than one of 14,000 vibrations to the second, unless we use tubes of still smaller bore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With a 0.16" inner tube (40 units) do not trust theoretical pitches for depths <60 units; expect a practical upper reliable test near 14,000 Hz unless smaller bores are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of perception near auditory limits and test positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When the limits of audibility are approached, the sound becomes much fainter, and when that limit is reached, the sound usually gives place to a peculiar sensation, which is not sound but more like dizziness ... The facility of hearing shrill sounds depends in some degree on the position of the whistle, for it is highest when it is held exactly opposite the opening of the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing high-frequency hearing limits, hold whistle directly opposite ear for maximum detectability; expect faintness near limits and possible non-auditory sensations (dizziness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting high-note hearing loss (nerve vs auditory canal)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the power of hearing high notes is wholly lost, the loss is commonly owing to failure in the nerves, but when very deaf people are still able to hear high notes if they are sounded with force, the nerves are usually all right, and the fault lies in the lining of the auditory canal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate nerve loss from canal blockage by testing with louder high notes: preserved perception at high intensity suggests canal issues rather than neural failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Illumination (mental image brightness)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Illumination.--Is the image dim or fairly clear? Is its brightness comparable to that of the actual scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask subjects to compare vividness/brightness of mental images to real scenes; record qualitative rating (dim → fairly clear → comparable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Definition (sharpness / focus of mental image)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. Definition.--Are all the objects pretty well defined at the same time, or is the place of sharpest definition at any one moment more contracted than it is in a real scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe whether subjects perceive uniform sharpness across the image or a narrower focus of clarity; note whether definition fluctuates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Colouring (accuracy of colours in imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. Colouring.--Are the colours of the china, of the toast, bread crust, mustard, meat, parsley, or whatever may have been on the table, quite distinct and natural?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether colours in recalled imagery are vivid and natural, and which elements are most/least vividly coloured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Extent of field of view
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. Extent of field of view.--Call up the image of some panoramic view (the walls of your room might suffice), can you force yourself to see mentally a wider range of it than could be taken in by any single glance of the eyes? Can you mentally see more than three faces of a die, or more than one hemisphere of a globe at the same instant of time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mental imagery can exceed an ocular single-glance field and whether simultaneous multiple facets can be visualised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Distance of images
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. Distance of images.--Where do mental images appear to be situated? within the head, within the eye-ball, just in front of the eyes, or at a distance corresponding to reality? Can you project an image upon a piece of paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the perceived spatial locus of images and whether subjects can externalise/projection onto surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Command over images (control and retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. Command over images.--Can you retain a mental picture steadily before the eyes? When you do so, does it grow brighter or dimmer? When the act of retaining it becomes wearisome, in what part of the head or eye-ball is the fatigue felt?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe subjects' capacity to voluntarily sustain images, changes in vividness over time, and location of any fatigue sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Persons (recall of faces and manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. Persons.--Can you recall with distinctness the features of all near relations and many other persons? Can you at will cause your mental image of any or most of them to sit, stand, or turn slowly round? Can you deliberately seat the image of a well-known person in a chair and see it with enough distinctness to enable you to sketch it leisurely (supposing yourself able to draw)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess facial recall fidelity and dynamic control (pose, rotation) to evaluate richness of person imagery; test ability to support detailed sketching from image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Scenery (precision of landscape imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. Scenery.--Do you preserve the recollection of scenery with much precision of detail, and do you find pleasure in dwelling on it? Can you easily form mental pictures from the descriptions of scenery that are so frequently met with in novels and books of travel?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported precision and enjoyment in recalling scenery as indicators of scene imagery strength and aptitude for imagery from verbal descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Comparison with reality (mistaking imagery for perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. Comparison with reality.--What difference do you perceive between a very vivid mental picture called up in the dark, and a real scene? Have you ever mistaken a mental image for a reality when in health and wide awake?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record qualitative differences and any history of confusions between vivid images and actual perception; flag any pathological confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Numerals and dates (associative imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. Numerals and dates.--Are these invariably associated in your mind with any peculiar mental imagery, whether of written or printed figures, diagrams, or colours? If so, explain fully, and say if you can account for the association?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe synesthetic or idiosyncratic imagery associated with numbers/dates and request explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Specialities (imagery in cognitive aptitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: 11. Specialities.--If you happen to have special aptitudes for mechanics, mathematics (either geometry of three dimensions or pure analysis), mental arithmetic, or chess-playing blindfold, please explain fully how far your processes depend on the use of visual images, and how far otherwise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask subjects with domain aptitudes to describe the role of visual imagery in problem-solving, to relate imagery strength to cognitive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Sensory-group ratings A–F
rubrics_metrics.description: 12. Call up before your imagination the objects specified in the six following paragraphs, numbered A to F, and consider carefully whether your mental representation of them generally, is in each group very faint, faint, fair, good, or vivid and comparable to the actual sensation: A. Light and colour; B. Sound; C. Smells; D. Tastes; E. Touch; F. Other sensations (Heat, hunger, cold, thirst, fatigue, fever, drowsiness, a bad cold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a graded scale (very faint → vivid/comparable) across multiple sensory modalities to profile multisensory imagery strength; provide examples under each category to standardise interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: Music (auditory imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: 13. Music.--Have you any aptitude for mentally recalling music, or for imagining it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe subjects' capacity for musical imagery and internal auditory rehearsal; note whether imagery is melodic, harmonic, or episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire dimension: At different ages (developmental change)
rubrics_metrics.description: 14. At different ages.--Do you recollect what your powers of visualising, etc., were in childhood? Have they varied much within your recollection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect retrospective reports on changes in imagery strength across lifespan to examine developmental or experiential effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire instruction: Supplementary information allowable
rubrics_metrics.description: General remarks.--Supplementary information written here, or on a separate piece of paper, will be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and encourage free-text supplementary comments to capture idiosyncratic phenomena or elaborations beyond the structured questions.
